Phase 1 metric results, with analysis

Final checkpoints (training step 9,156, about 150M training tokens each). Each section says what the metric measures, gives the results, and ends with an analysis (blue box). The overall view is at the end. Raw values: final_metrics_raw_results.csv.

The five models

ModelWhat it is
PKM, learned keys, seed 0, seed 1, seed 2The main model: a 6-layer GPT with a product-key memory (PKM) layer at layer 3. Each token's query is matched against learned keys; the best-matching slots are read and their values are added to the token's representation. Keys, queries and values all train. Three training seeds.
PKM, frozen random keys, seed 0Same as the main model, but the keys are frozen at their random starting values. Queries and values still train, so the model can still use the memory but cannot move the keys.
Dense, no memory layerSame network with an ordinary feed-forward layer at layer 3 instead of the memory, sized for the same compute per token.

Where the numbers come from

  • Held-out text. For each of the five Pile subjects (FreeLaw, Github, Pile-CC, PubMed Central, Wikipedia), a set of documents was kept out of training entirely. It is split into two halves: a discovery half, used only to choose slots (U4 ranking for E1), and a test half, used to score (Q1, E1). A test never reuses text that chose its slots.
  • Biographies. Made-up people with five facts each (birth date, birth city, university, major, employer). People are in four exposure tiers by how often their biography appeared in training: frequent (~300 copies), normal (~100), rare (~30), control (never). Each fact has 8 prompts: 2 discovery and 2 test prompts in training wordings, and 4 paraphrase prompts in wordings never used in training.
  • Official numbers (Q1, Q2) are each training run's own final evaluation: the whole test half (about 2.5M tokens per subject) and every person.
  • Slice numbers (everything else) come from metrics.py on a fixed sample, the same for every model: 64 test-half documents per subject, first 256 tokens of each (about 72k tokens in all); 80 frequent people and 10 per other tier (all 8 prompts of every fact). The slice is smaller because the removal tests (E1, E2) rerun the model many times.
  • "Learned seeds: mean [min, max]" column = the average of the three learned-key models (seeds 0, 1, 2), with the lowest and highest of the three in brackets.

Analysis

All five runs trained normally: losses stayed finite, fell by about 67% from initialization, and were at their lowest at the end. Memory coverage is 100% and frequent-tier facts are recalled 117–185× more often than control facts.

The single red cell is learned s2's spike ratio of 1.535 at step 9,050, just over the 1.5 limit. The other runs peak at 1.41–1.48. It is one noisy training batch near the end, and s2's held-out loss and fact recall are in line with s0 and s1, so s2 is kept in the 3-seed analysis with this flag (decided with Roie).

Held-out loss still fell 1.6–1.7% over the last 2,000 steps in every run, so the models are close to, but not fully at, convergence. The same is true for all five, so comparisons between them are fair.

Q1: next-token quality on held-out text

What it measures. How well each model predicts the next token in text it never trained on: the average loss (negative log-probability of the true next token, in nats; lower is better), per subject and averaged. Perplexity is eloss. Official numbers: whole test half, ~2.5M tokens per subject.

PubMed Central3.5763.5793.5863.5813.650

Average next-token top-1 accuracy0.41490.41420.41410.41440.4078
USPTO loss (subject never in training)4.5224.5444.5344.5244.586

Analysis

The memory layer helps at equal compute. Every PKM model beats dense on every subject, by 0.05–0.08 nats/token (average perplexity 42.0–42.4 against 45.0). The gain also holds on USPTO, a subject none of the models trained on, but it is smaller there: 0.042–0.065 nats (learned-seed mean 0.053) against a 0.059–0.068 average on the trained subjects. The drop varies by seed: s0 and random keys lose almost nothing (0.065 and 0.062), while s1's USPTO gain (0.042) is below its gain on every trained subject. Part of the memory's benefit is therefore specific to the subjects it was trained on.

Learning the keys makes no difference to quality. The random-key model (3.743) falls inside the learned seeds' range (3.739–3.748) on the average and on every subject. Seed-to-seed differences between the learned models are about 0.01 nats.

Q2: fact recall

What it measures. The model gets a biography sentence cut just before a fact ("… was born in") and scores every possible value of that attribute (100–300 candidates: 200 birth dates, 200 cities, 300 universities, 100 majors, 250 employers). Top-1 accuracy: how often the true value scores highest. Mean rank: the true value's average position in that ranked list (1 = top; about half the list size = no knowledge). Training wording = the 2 test prompts; new wording = the 4 paraphrase prompts.

Analysis

Fact recall depends strongly on exposure. In training wording it is about 0.88 for frequent people, 0.43 for normal, 0.04 for rare, and at chance (0.005) for never-seen controls.

The memory matters most for the middle tier. Dense recalls 0.75 of frequent facts but only 0.13 of normal ones, against about 0.43 for PKM. The memory lets the model store facts it saw about 100 times, which dense mostly cannot.

Recall does not carry over to new wordings: top-1 is about 0.11 for frequent people in every model, dense included. The true value still ranks well above chance (mean rank about 64 against about 105 for controls), so the model knows the association weakly but stores it tied to the sentence form. This matches the data-check note in the plan.

Random keys recall slightly less than the learned seeds (0.850 against 0.871–0.892 for frequent), a small gap.

U1: how many memory slots are used (diagnostic)

What it measures. The memory has 65,536 slots; each token reads 128 of them (32 per head, 4 heads). On the slice text: the share of slots read at least once, the share that is ever a token's single highest-weighted slot, and the KL divergence of the read distribution from perfectly even use (0 = even).

Learned s0Learned s1Learned s2Random keys
Slots read at least once99.93%99.94%99.96%99.97%
Slots ever ranked first21.3%22.4%22.3%19.8%
KL to even use (bits)0.7340.7180.7100.779

Analysis

Almost every slot is read (99.9%), so there are no dead slots. Only 20–22% of slots are ever a token's top choice, so most slots serve as secondary contributors.

Learned keys use slots slightly less evenly than random keys (KL 0.71–0.73 against 0.78 bits), but the difference is small. Neither looks collapsed.

U4: do slots specialize by subject?

What it measures. Whether knowing which slot was read tells you which subject the text is from, beyond what the token itself already tells you. Many words are typical of one subject (e.g. def in Github), so a slot that simply serves that word would look subject-specific. U4 removes that by comparing reads of the same token across subjects.

Example. Take the token court. Suppose it appears in FreeLaw and in Wikipedia text. If in FreeLaw documents it mostly reads slots {12, 870, 4031} and in Wikipedia documents mostly {55, 902, 7718}, then the slot reveals the subject even though the token is the same: high U4. If it reads the same slots wherever it appears, U4 is zero for that token. U4 averages this over all tokens, as the mutual information between slot and subject given the token (bits).

Shuffle baseline. Even with no specialization the estimate is above zero by chance. So the subject labels are shuffled between whole documents 99 times and U4 recomputed each time. Excess = real value − shuffle average. p = share of shuffles at least as high as the real value (0.01 = none of 99).

Rows of the table:

  • U4, real: the slot–subject mutual information given the token, measured with the true subject labels.
  • U4, shuffled average: the same quantity after randomly reassigning subject labels between whole documents, averaged over 99 shuffles. This is what chance alone gives.
  • Excess: real − shuffled average. The part of U4 that is due to actual subject specialization.
  • p: share of the 99 shuffles that reached the real value or higher (plus one, divided by 100). 0.01 means no shuffle reached it.
Learned s0Learned s1Learned s2Random keysLearned seeds: mean [min, max]
U4, real (bits)0.6370.6490.6370.6220.641 [0.637, 0.649]
U4, shuffled average (bits)0.4690.4660.4720.4710.469 [0.466, 0.472]
Excess (bits)0.16890.18350.16510.15190.1725 [0.1651, 0.1835]
p (99 shuffles)0.010.010.010.01

Analysis

Slots do carry subject information beyond the token. In every model the real value is far above all 99 shuffles (p = 0.01, the smallest possible). The excess is about 0.17 bits, roughly a quarter of the measured 0.64 bits; the rest is what the estimator gives by chance at this sample size.

Learned keys are a little more subject-specific than random keys (0.165–0.184 against 0.152). Random keys still show most of the effect, though, because the queries and values learn even when the keys cannot move.

E1: switching off a subject's slots

What it measures. Whether a subject's own slots matter more to that subject than to the others. For each subject: take its m most subject-specific slots (ranked on the discovery half), switch them off (value set to zero), and measure on the test half how much the loss rises on that subject minus how much it rises on the other subjects. Then do the same with m random slots chosen to match the real ones in how often they are read and how large their output is. Reported: real − random. Above zero = the subject depends on its own slots more than chance.

Example (learned s0, FreeLaw, m = 64). Switching off FreeLaw's top 64 slots raised FreeLaw's loss by 0.0246 nats/token and the other subjects' by -0.0000 on average, a gap of 0.0246. Three matched random sets of 64 slots gave an average gap of 0.0009. Result: 0.0237 nats.

Run at m = 16, 64 (main) and 256 slots. "n/a" = no set of random slots matched that subject's slots closely enough, so that subject has no result for that model and is left out of its average.

Sampling note: in the sample-size pilot, redrawing the documents moved the 64-slot value by about 1/2.3 of the smallest seed value, so part of the spread between seeds is sampling noise.

Analysis

Removing a subject's own slots hurts that subject more than matched random slots do, in every subject and model where a control was found. So the subject-specific slots U4 finds are also used.

The effect is small. Switching off 64 of 65,536 slots (0.1%) costs about 0.008 nats on average, against 0.8 nats for switching off the whole layer.

It grows roughly in proportion to the number of slots removed: 0.002 at 16, 0.008 at 64, 0.034 at 256, about ×4 per ×4. There is no sign of a small set of critical subject slots that would make the first 16 matter most. Subject knowledge looks spread over many slots, each contributing a little.

FreeLaw stands out (0.017–0.024), so legal text has the most specialized slots. The missing FreeLaw (s1) and Github (s2) values pull those seeds' averages around, and the pilot showed part of the seed spread is sampling noise. Treat the seed-to-seed ordering as unreliable.

E2: are single facts stored in a few slots?

What it measures. For each fact, the slots its prompts read are switched off one at a time, most-used first, until the model's recall of that fact on the test prompts drops to chance, up to 16 slots. If that happens, those slots are the fact's core set; core fraction = core set size ÷ slots the fact reads. As a check, the same number of random slots from the fact's own reads (matched for read count and output size) are switched off instead; control erasure rate = how often that also erases the fact. Run on the 339 facts that all four PKM models recall, so every model is tested on the same facts.

Each of the 339 facts ends in one of three outcomes (bars and first three table rows):

  • Fact erased, control done: switching off some of the fact's slots (16 or fewer) made the model lose the fact, and we could also find a matching set of random slots (same number, similar read counts and output sizes, taken from the fact's own reads) to switch off for comparison. Only these facts get a core fraction and a control erasure rate.
  • Fact erased, no control found: the fact was lost within 16 slots, but no matching random set could be found (the core slots were unusually busy or large compared with the fact's other slots), so there is no comparison for it.
  • Not erased within 16 slots: the 16 most-used slots were switched off and the model still recalled the fact above chance. The search stops at 16, so these facts' core sets, if any, are larger than 16 slots.
  • Core fraction: for facts in the first group, the number of slots that erased the fact ÷ the number of slots the fact reads, averaged.
  • Control erasure rate: for the same facts, how often switching off the matched random slots also erased the fact.

Sampling note: in the pilot, E2's sampling spread was larger than a third of its seed spread (about 1.6×).

Analysis

For most facts there is no small core set within 16 slots. 294–299 of the 339 facts survive having their 16 most-used slots switched off. A fact's prompts read a couple of hundred distinct slots (249 for the single-slot example on s0), and the erased facts' cores are about 2.5% of what they read, so 16 slots is a small slice of what a fact uses.

A minority of facts do behave like the library picture: 19–40 per learned seed are erased by a handful of slots. Matched random slots rarely erase them (2–7%), so those slots really are specific to the fact.

Random keys have far fewer such facts: 7, against 19–40.

Limit: the search stops at 16 slots. Earlier work found fact core sets of 100–500 slots, so "not erased within 16" means larger than 16, not "no core set". These counts are small, and the pilot found E2's seed spread to be mostly sampling noise.

V2: is a read dominated by one value?

What it measures. A memory read adds up 128 weighted values. V2 asks how much of that sum comes from the largest single value (and the two largest), as a share of the output, on held-out text and on fact prompts. It also measures whether values read together point in similar directions: mean cosine between co-read values minus that of random pairs with the same sizes (alignment; 0 = no more aligned than chance).

Analysis

Reads are not dominated by one value. The largest of 128 values carries 7–9% of a read's output and the two largest 12–15%, so the remaining 126 values make up most of it. This is the spread pattern, not the library one.

Learned keys concentrate reads more than random keys: 0.074 against 0.060 on text and 0.084 against 0.057 on facts, a clear gap (see X2). With learned keys, fact prompts are more concentrated than text; with random keys they are not.

Co-read values are only slightly more aligned than chance (cosine excess 0.01–0.02), the same with random keys. So the values are mostly building outputs together rather than acting as redundant copies.

X2: learned keys vs frozen random keys

What it measures. Whether learning the keys changes the main results. We have three learned-key seeds but only one random-key model, so the comparison uses the seeds' own variation as the yardstick: for each metric, the margin is the full range of the three learned seeds (highest − lowest), fixed before the random-key model was scored. If the random-key value is within one margin of the learned mean, it counts as inside (no difference larger than seed-to-seed variation); otherwise outside.

Example (U4 excess). Learned seeds 0.1689, 0.1835, 0.1651: mean 0.1725, margin 0.0185. Random keys 0.1519, which is 0.0206 below the mean, more than one margin, so: outside.

E1 and E2 have no margin: each seed's E1 average is over a different set of subjects (s1 lacks FreeLaw, s2 lacks Github), and each seed's E2 average is over a different set of erased facts, so the seeds' values are not directly comparable.

Analysis

Learning the keys leaves quality unchanged and concentrates reads. The concentration (all four V2 share numbers, 2.8–3.5 margins outside) is the clearest difference between the two key types in the whole study.

The subject-specificity difference (U4) is just outside the margin, at 1.1×. The plan says to add 1–2 random-key seeds before deciding a case this close to the edge.

Alignment between co-read values is the same for both.

E1 and E2 cannot be judged by the rule, because each seed is averaged over different subjects or facts. Descriptively, random keys sit inside the learned E1 range and have fewer erasable facts in E2 (7 against 19–40). The latter points the same way as V2: learned keys make storage somewhat more localized.

One random-key seed is a real limit: its own seed noise is unknown.

Whole memory layer off. How it is done: in the trained model, every one of the 65,536 memory slots is switched off at once, the same way single slots are switched off in E1 and E2 (the slot's value is set to zero after the key search, so each read returns zero). The memory layer then adds nothing to a token's representation; every other layer is unchanged and nothing is retrained. Analysis

C6. The value table is nearly full-rank: about 366 of 384 directions, the same for every model. On 896 rows it measures 342, close to the dense layer's 335. There is no low-dimensional structure, and the stored values are about as varied as an ordinary feed-forward layer.

C4. The busiest slots write function words and punctuation (the, and, of, commas), so the most-read slots are general-purpose and not topical.

Whole layer off. Removing the memory costs 0.81–0.84 nats/token for learned keys and 0.74 for random keys. That is far more than the 0.07 the memory gains over dense, because the network was trained with the memory and relies on it in place of a feed-forward layer. Frequent-fact recall falls from about 0.90 to about 0.30, so about two thirds of fact recall runs through the memory layer. FreeLaw is hit hardest (1.13), matching E1.

Resources. The memory adds 96 MiB of parameters (209 against 113 MiB) and about 25% latency on this Mac for its quality gain.

Overall view

What the memory does. At equal compute, a PKM memory layer makes the model better at language modeling (0.05–0.08 nats on every subject, including one it never saw) and much better at storing facts seen a moderate number of times. Normal-tier recall is about 0.43 against 0.13 for dense. The network relies on it heavily: switching it off costs 0.8 nats and two thirds of fact recall.

How it stores knowledge: mostly spread, with a weak library-like tilt.

  • H1 (subjects). Supported but weak. Slots carry subject information beyond the word (U4, highly significant), and removing a subject's slots hurts it specifically (E1). But the effect is small, grows evenly with the number of slots removed, and is concentrated in one subject (FreeLaw). Subject knowledge is spread over many slots that each lean toward a subject, not kept in a few dedicated ones.
  • H2 (facts). Not supported at the depth tested. About 87% of facts survive removal of their 16 most-used slots, and facts read a couple of hundred slots each. A minority (6–12% per seed) do have small, fact-specific core sets. Whether the rest have core sets of 100+ slots, as in earlier work, is untested with the 16-slot limit.
  • H4 (reads). Not supported. A read is built from many values, with the largest carrying under a tenth of the output. Co-read values are mostly not redundant copies.
  • H3 (learned keys). Partly supported. Learning the keys does not change quality, but it makes reads clearly more concentrated (V2), slightly more subject-specific (U4, borderline), and gives more facts with small core sets (E2, descriptive). What learned keys add is a move toward the library picture, not the picture itself.

How much to trust this. Q1, Q2, U4 and V2 are stable: seed-to-seed spread is small and the pilot showed sampling noise well below it. E1 and E2 are noisier: part of their seed spread is sampling noise, E1 lost one subject in two seeds, and E2 rests on 7–40 facts per model. X2 has a single random-key seed, and its U4 result sits at the edge of the margin. One learned seed (s2) has a borderline training-check failure.

Open points within the current plan. The plan already calls for 1–2 more random-key seeds when X2 lands near the edge, as U4 does here. E2's 16-slot search limit is what leaves most facts unresolved, so a larger limit is the setting to revisit if H2 is to be answered for most facts. Neither would change any metric's design.
